passage: On Saturday five-year-old Sumit sat pressed against his father Lalit, a blanket up to his nose. Two nights ago a cartoon monster had leapt out of a cupboard, and Sumit had woken twice since, crying. Lalit switched the show off. "It's a story, and you're safe," he said, and promised a funny film with popcorn instead. Across the room, Sumit's friend Vaibhav wore a towel as a cape, shouting his cartoon hero's catch-phrase and trying the spinning kick. "I'm flying!" Lalit grinned, then told him gently, "Your hero can do that on the screen. Real people can't fly, so no jumping off the sofa." Vaibhav hopped down and bowed. Later, a game on the tablet opened a chat window: "Send me a photo, and don't tell your parents." Vaibhav ran to Lalit with the tablet held out. "Good that you showed me," Lalit said, and closed the chat. Beside them Meher had watched cartoons all morning, and when her mother said the show was over, Meher wailed. Her mother knelt and said, "Let's go to the balcony and blow bubbles."

qa.q: What did Vaibhav wear as a cape?
qa.a: He wore a towel as a cape.

qa.q: How did Lalit's response to Sumit's fear differ from his response to Vaibhav's game chat, and what rule did the second show?
qa.a: For Sumit he switched off the show and said it was a story and he was safe; for Vaibhav he closed the chat because the boy showed him at once, which shows that any request for a photo or secrecy should always go to a trusted adult.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling after the monster scene, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He was frightened; he had woken twice crying and sat pressed against his father with a blanket up to his nose.

qa.q: What helped Meher after the show ended?
qa.a: Her mother knelt and offered a fun next thing, blowing bubbles on the balcony, so Meher had something to move on to.

grounding: Four small children around screens show fear from a scary scene, a stranger's secret request, admiration for a cartoon hero and wailing when the show ends.

passage: At the temple committee dinner, an uncle told Ramesh he was wandering from the path and should think of his mother's shame. Ramesh left the hall with a lump in his throat. He had stopped going to the morning prayer weeks ago and missed the smell of camphor, the singing, the way everyone stood together. The grief for it was real. At the office, his colleague Parveen laughed when he mentioned he still lit a lamp on Thursdays. "You believe in that? It is just superstition." The words stung, and Ramesh felt ready to snap back. Instead he said briefly, "It matters to me. Please leave the jokes out." Parveen shrugged. Weeks later, Nirmala, who followed no religion, asked him over tea, "What does the lamp mean to you? I am not trying to change your mind." Ramesh spoke about his grandmother and the quiet the lamp gave him, and Nirmala listened without arguing, then told him what she found meaningful in volunteering at the food bank. He went along the next Sunday. There, and later at a small reading group that welcomed questions, he found company that did not need him to have all the answers.

qa.q: What did Ramesh miss about the morning prayer?
qa.a: He missed the smell of camphor, the singing and the way everyone stood together.

qa.q: How did Parveen's comment about the lamp differ from Nirmala's question, and how did Ramesh respond to each?
qa.a: Parveen called it superstition, which stung, and Ramesh answered briefly and asked for no jokes; Nirmala asked what the lamp meant without trying to change his mind, and Ramesh spoke about his grandmother and the quiet it gave him.

qa.q: What might Ramesh have been feeling when he left the hall after the uncle's words?
qa.a: He was probably hurt and ashamed, with a sense of losing his place, since he left with a lump in his throat.

qa.q: What did Ramesh find that helps with the loss of his old community?
qa.a: He found the food bank and a small reading group that welcomed questions, where he did not need to have all the answers.

grounding: One man drifting from belief meets mockery, an elder's lecture, grief for lost ritual, and a friend of no faith who asks honest questions.

passage: Jatin rehearsed one sentence for three weeks and froze each time Meghna walked into the library. He pictured everyone laughing. Finally he said it once, plainly: "Would you like to get coffee sometime, as more than friends?" Meghna's smile was kind. "I like you a lot as a friend, but I don't feel that way. I'm sorry." It stung, and Jatin felt it for days, but she had left no false hope and he chased none. In their flat, Gautam kept refreshing Sara's profile at midnight, guessing at her moods. Farhan noticed. "You have looked at that phone forty times tonight. Come and play football tomorrow." Gautam grumbled, went, and slept better. Farhan himself had been talking for months to Leena in another city; her photos were sunny and her messages perfect, and he had built her from highlights. When she visited, they had chai at a crowded stall. She was late, spilled her tea and argued about films. He laughed. She was funnier and messier than the screen, and he liked her at least as much.

qa.q: Where did Farhan and Leena have chai?
qa.a: They had chai at a crowded stall.

qa.q: How did Jatin's way of dealing with his feelings differ from Gautam's?
qa.a: Jatin said his sentence once, plainly, and accepted Meghna's kind no, while Gautam kept refreshing Sara's profile at midnight and guessing at her moods until Farhan invited him to play football.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling for the three weeks before he asked?
qa.a: He was afraid of humiliation; he froze whenever Meghna walked in and pictured everyone laughing.

qa.q: What could Gautam do next besides football?
qa.a: He could keep widening his life with friends and activities and talk to Farhan about the loop of thoughts, instead of checking Sara's profile.

grounding: Four young men show a crush met with fear of asking, an idealised online image, a kind rejection, and midnight profile-checking.

passage: Seema's father, Samir, went silent for three days whenever she mentioned renting a flat near her new office. Then he spoke of his heart and how a daughter should think of her father's health. Seema felt guilty for wanting her own place. When she reminded him that last month he had told her not to come home late, he snapped, "I never said that. You are too sensitive." She stopped arguing. Later she opened the notes on her phone, where she had written dates and his exact words, and trusted them. At a family wedding her uncle Karthik loudly asked what she earned and why she was not married yet. "I'm doing well, and I'm not discussing it," she said with a smile, and walked to the buffet. Weeks later Samir showed her the old tin trunk from his village days and mentioned the year he skipped meals so his brothers could study. Seema felt her chest soften. It did not excuse the silences. "Papa, I love you, and I am still moving out in March. You can visit every Sunday."

qa.q: What did Seema keep in the notes on her phone?
qa.a: She kept dates and her father's exact words.

qa.q: How did Seema's response to her father's guilt and denial differ from her response to her uncle's questions?
qa.a: With Samir she trusted her notes and calmly stated her plan while staying warm, and with Karthik she answered briefly with a smile and walked away.

qa.q: What did Seema feel when Samir showed her the old trunk and spoke of skipping meals?
qa.a: Her chest softened with sadness and tenderness, though understanding him did not excuse the silences.

qa.q: What could Seema do to keep both warmth and boundaries?
qa.a: She could keep inviting him for Sunday visits, stick to her plan to move out, and keep her notes.

grounding: One adult child meets a parent's guilt-driven control, denial, a relative's comparison, and later sees the parent's own hardship while keeping boundaries.

passage: On Monday Parveen, two, sat on the little red potty and, with a surprised look, produced a puddle. "You did it!" said her father, Vishal, clapping softly, and Parveen beamed and asked to sit again. On Tuesday there was an accident on the rug. Her grandfather Uday laughed and said, "Ew, dirty girl!" Parveen's face crumpled, and for the rest of the week she hid behind the sofa whenever she felt the urge. Vishal quietly told Uday, "Please don't laugh. It makes her hide." On Wednesday he calmly wiped the floor with her. "It's okay. Bodies take time. We will try again another day." By Friday Parveen stood with her arms folded and shouted "No potty!", holding her legs tight. Vishal did not push. "Would you like the red one or the blue one? Or shall we try tomorrow?" Parveen looked at both. "Tomorrow," she said.

qa.q: What colour was the potty Parveen first used?
qa.a: It was the little red potty.

qa.q: How did Uday's reaction to the accident differ from Vishal's, and what did Parveen do afterwards?
qa.a: Uday laughed and called her dirty, and Parveen hid behind the sofa whenever she felt the urge, while Vishal calmly wiped the floor with her, said it was okay and offered to try again another day.

qa.q: What was Parveen probably feeling while she hid behind the sofa?
qa.a: She was probably ashamed and worried about making a mistake, since her face crumpled when Uday laughed and she hid afterwards.

qa.q: What could the adults do when Parveen shouts "No potty!"?
qa.a: They could offer choices like the red or blue potty, keep it low-key, and pause until tomorrow if she is not ready.

grounding: One toddler's toilet training brings cheerful praise, a laugh at an accident that teaches hiding, calm clean-up, and refusal met with choices.

passage: Jagdish built a tower of twelve blocks all by himself and shouted, "Look at me! Look!" His mother, Aditi, came over. "You stacked the big ones at the bottom and stayed patient when it wobbled. You worked hard on that." Jagdish felt tall and happy and started a second tower. At school he pinned his new reading badge on his shirt and showed his friend Manav, who looked away, lips pressed. Jagdish felt confused. Then he said, "You can get one too. What are you making?" Manav pulled out his drawing of a train, Jagdish admired it, and they shared a bench. That evening he held up a photo of his tower for his sister Jasleen. "Mine is better," Jasleen said, sliding her own drawing next to it. Jagdish felt small. Aditi noticed. "Jagdish's tower took patience, and Jasleen, your drawing has such careful colours. Both are wonderful in different ways." Both children grinned.

qa.q: How many blocks were in Jagdish's tower?
qa.a: The tower had twelve blocks.

qa.q: How did Jagdish handle Manav looking away differently from Jasleen's "Mine is better"?
qa.a: With Manav, Jagdish said he could get a badge too and asked about his drawing, keeping the friendship warm, while with Jasleen he felt small until Aditi praised each child for their own work.

qa.q: How did Jagdish feel when Manav looked away, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt confused, since he did not understand why his friend looked away with pressed lips after he showed the badge.

qa.q: What could Jagdish say next time Jasleen says hers is better?
qa.a: He could point out something he likes about her drawing and still enjoy his own tower, without turning it into a contest. 🙂

grounding: A five-year-old's pride is met by a mother's descriptive praise, a friend who looks away, and a sister's claim that hers is better.
